newsitem.title: UK: UK's PowderJect aims for 35 million stg injection.
newsitem.headline: UK's PowderJect aims for 35 million stg injection.

text.p: A British company developing needle-free injections which shoot into the skin at 1700 miles an hour said on Tuesday it hoped to raise 35 million pounds ($57.5 million) when it floats on the stock market next month.
PowderJect Pharmaceuticals Plc, which is the latest drug flotation to evolve from work at Oxford University, said a successful launch would value it at around 110 million stg.

At the centre of the company's hopes is a six inch-long suppository-shaped device which fires powdered drugs into the skin at supersonic speed. PowderJect claims that the system, which doesn't rely on needles, is painless and causes no skin damage.

PowderJect founder and chief executive officer Paul Drayson, who said when he first saw the prototype technology in 1993 "it looked like a Bazooka and sounded like a Bazooka," told journalists that "the Holy Grail of the (drugs) industry is to come up with a system which represents efficacy and ease of use."
With PowderJect, a high pressure helium cylinder which is being produced by gases specialist BOC Group Plc accelerates fine drug particles to Mach 3, three times the speed of sound.

"This is rocket science," PowderJect's head of product development Terry Burkoth said at the launch of the flotation prospectus. But despite the complex technology, the company claims it "can be used by anyone," making it ideal for people such as diabetics who have to inject themselves regularly with insulin.
A second system is being developed to inject drugs into the side of the mouth, suitable for speeding up the impact of migraine drugs and anaesthetics.

PowderJect, which used to be known as Oxford Biosciences, stressed however that it was not a technology company, and has set its sights on getting a major chunk of the profits from drugs administered with the system. It is deliberately keeping the costs of the devices to levels comparable with existing pre-filled syringes.

Scientists in Oxford, San Francisco and Wisconsin are also developing products based on generic drugs, including one to treat male impotence which analysts said could have particular promise. PowderJect also announced an impressive string of blue chip collaborators including Roche Holdings AG and Pfizer Inc.

SmithKline Beecham Plc is also believed to be on board, working on its new genital warts drug, as is U.S. biotech giant Amgen Inc, which has an important injectable anaemia drug, Epogen. And Powderject is collaborating on injectable anaesthetics with Britain's Chiroscience Group Plc .
A third area of focus is gene-based vaccines, including one for Hepatitis B now in clinical trials.

One analyst said the technology is "very interesting because there are a number of drugs which would benefit from a non-syringe injection." However the company is thought to have a number of problems to overcome, such as skin irritation and the breakdown of large molecules such as insulin under the high-speed pressure.
Nomura analyst Nick Woolf said the 110 million pounds valuation on the group was high given that significant products and break-even are some years away.

"I was impressed by the product, the patent position, the management and the clients they have got on board," said Woolf, but he added that his advice to clients would be "that you don't have to rush in at the IPO."
